episodes.211996: Thunderstorms developed north of a warm front during the afternoon hours on Sunday (5/17).  The strongest storms produced hail up to penny size and damaging winds across east-central Wisconsin, causing over $100,000 worth of damage in Two Rivers.
episodes.211997: A thunderstorm produced strong winds over Lake Michigan during the afternoon hours on Sunday (5/17).
episodes.212011: During the late afternoon, and into the evening, numerous thunderstorms formed over Northwest Kansas in the vicinity of a sharpening dryline. One of them produced hail up to baseball size over and near Goodland. This same storm also produced wind gusts over 80 mph at the Goodland airport. The storm near Goodland produced a brief tornado southwest of Edson as it merged with another storm. As thunderstorms moved eastward, they continued to produce straight-line winds across Thomas, Sheridan, Graham, Norton, and Gove counties.  Over 40 power poles were snapped in Sheridan County, and a machine shed north of Hoxie sustained damage.  Dust storm conditions were reported on the south edge of the thunderstorm activity as the storms moved east over northern Gove County.
episodes.212275: A thunderstorms tracked east across northeast Elbert and northern Lincoln Counties producing wind gusts up to 70 mph.
episodes.212294: A warm front lifted into the Ohio Valley region, producing showers and thunderstorms. Some of these storms produced damaging wind gusts.
episodes.212402: An approaching mid-level disturbance broke a weak cap and allowed storms to erupt during the afternoon along a slow moving frontal boundary. These storms rapidly organized into short bowing segments and then became highly linear across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota during the evening. Initial supercell storms produced large hail with as much as 2000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE, but DCAPE of around 750-1000 J/kg allowed for the development of organized cold pools and an increasing wind threat. Several brief and highly visible tornadic spin-ups developed along the line of storms by late afternoon and evening across far eastern South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.||In addition, repeated thunderstorms brought as much as 2-4 inches of rain in a short period of time to portions of Plymouth and southern Sioux County in northwest Iowa. This same area had also received locally heavy rainfall during the previous days, resulting in spotty flooding of already saturated locations.
episodes.212652: Thunderstorms trained over portions of Barton, Russell, Ellsworth, and Lincoln counties during the afternoon and evening hours of May 17th. Several reports of large hail and flash flooding were received. The largest hail report was near Milberger in Russell County with a size of 2.25 inches in diameter.
episodes.212792: A summer-like pattern including high CAPE/low shear and both Gulf Coast and Atlantic Coast sea breezes resulted in numerous convection across interior northeast FL and southeast GA. Pockets of dry air aloft as well as cooler than normal mid level temperatures resulted in isolated severe wind gusts as well as small hail. Slow storm motion also produced localized very heavy rainfall.
episodes.212966: A line of thunderstorms developed during the late morning hours of May 17th across northwestern Nebraska. As this activity tracked east into north central Nebraska, it became severe as it approached Brown and Keya Paha Counties during the early afternoon hours. This line of strong to severe thunderstorms tracked further east, impacting Rock, Boyd and Holt Counties before exiting the area. Thunderstorm wind gusts to 77 MPH and wind damage to a convenience store were reported with the strongest storms.
episodes.213179: Two rounds of severe storms developed across north-central Kansas on the evening of May 16. The first was a cluster of supercells that produced large to very large hail and isolated strong winds, while the second was a line of storms that mostly produced damaging winds.
episodes.213424: During the afternoon and evening hours of May 16, 2026, severe thunderstorms produced large hail, damaging wind gusts, and flash flooding across eastern Nebraska. The storms initiated along a frontal boundary draped across the region as a shortwave disturbance pivoted overhead. Earlier in the day, this shortwave had helped develop a surface low near the Colorado/western Nebraska border, which subsequently tracked eastward toward the Mid-Missouri Valley. Ahead of the low, an axis of 2,000 to 3,000 J/kg of MLCAPE developed near the boundary. This instability, combined with increasing deep-layer shear, created an environment highly supportive of strong to severe thunderstorms.||Sinitially presenting a significant large hail threat before transitioning into a destructive wind event. Through the early to mid-evening hours, widespread hail ranging from quarter (1.00 inch) to baseball (2.75 inches) size bombarded Platte, Saline, Seward, Gage, Lancaster, and Jefferson counties. The most intense hail occurred in Jefferson and Saline counties, highlighted by 2.75-inch hailstones measured near Plymouth and 2.50-inch hailstones reported near De Witt.||As the storms progressed into the late evening and early morning hours of May 17, the primary hazard shifted to severe and damaging straight-line winds. Jefferson County absorbed the brunt of this impact, with multiple mesonet stations and emergency management officials measuring extreme wind gusts between 75 and 88 mph in and around Fairbury. These intense winds caused significant impacts, including downed trees, widespread power outages, and near-zero visibility. The line of storms maintained severe intensity as it pushed eastward, producing gusts in excess of 60 mph across Gage and Richardson counties before eventually clearing the region.||In addition to the severe weather, repeated rounds of heavy rainfall brought flash flooding to southeast Nebraska, primarily impacting Gage, Johnson, Jefferson, and Saline counties. Widespread precipitation totals of 2 to 4 inches were observed across the region, with localized maximums of 5.80 to 7.00 inches concentrated in Gage County.
episodes.213440: During the late afternoon hours on the 17th, an isolated severe thunderstorm moved east across east-central Colorado, ahead of a strong cold front approaching from the northwest. Wind gusts up to 74 mph and hail up to ping-pong ball size were both reported in Kit Carson County.
episodes.213442: During the early evening hours on the 17th, an isolated severe thunderstorm moved east out of east-central Colorado and into northwest Kansas, ahead of a strong cold front approaching from the northwest. Large hail up to ping-pong ball size was reported in Sherman County.
episodes.213477: Severe thunderstorms north of M-46 produced over half a dozen reports of large hail.
episodes.213516: Severe thunderstorms produced hail, damaging wind gusts, and tornadoes across eastern Nebraska on May 17, 2026. On this day, an upper-level trough axis remained well to the west, but an embedded shortwave and attendant jet streak ejected from eastern Colorado into eastern Nebraska. At the surface, an elongated trough extended from a low in southeast Colorado through south-central Nebraska into southeast South Dakota, acting as a persistent focus for strong deep moist convergence. During the afternoon, a narrow dryline surged into central Nebraska and Kansas. East of the boundary, warm-sector dewpoints recovered into the mid-to-upper 60s, yielding a highly unstable environment with 3,000 to 4,000 J/kg of MLCAPE. Although mid-level winds were somewhat weak���resulting in unimpressive 0���6 km bulk shear���low-level hodographs featured ample cyclonic curvature. This provided sufficient low-level shear to keep updrafts organized and separated from downdrafts despite the weaker flow aloft.||A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across east-central Nebraska during the afternoon, pushing eastwards and growing upscale into a formidable wind-producing convective system. The storms initially presented a mixed hazard of large hail and damaging winds as they impacted counties including Madison, Platte, Cuming, and Saline. Hail up to golf ball size (1.75 inches) was reported near Wisner, while quarter-size hail fell in several surrounding communities. Three EF-1 tornadoes were also confirmed across eastern Nebraska in Thurston, Saunders and Cass county. However, severe straight-line winds quickly became the dominant threat. Wind gusts consistently measured between 60 and 70 mph caused widespread tree damage, snapping large branches with noticeable tree damage reported in communities like Friend, Crete, and Fairbury.||As the line surged eastward through the mid-to-late evening, the severe wind threat pushed straight through the Lincoln and Omaha metropolitan areas before crossing the Missouri River into western Iowa. An automated station at the Lincoln Airport measured a 68 mph wind gust, while emergency managers and spotters reported 70 mph gusts across Lancaster and Sarpy counties. These intense winds resulted in minor structural damage, including a torn gutter on a home in Lincoln and a damaged street light in La Vista. The Omaha Eppley Airfield recorded a 63 mph gust as the storms swept through the metro. By late evening, the system accelerated across southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, producing severe wind gusts of 71 mph in Pawnee County, Nebraska, before finally weakening and exiting the region.
episodes.213569: Clusters of showers and thunderstorms moved across portions of southwest Georgia ahead of a frontal boundary.  A few storms were severe with hail and wind damage.
episodes.213589: A cluster of thunderstorms developing and propagating northward across southwest Florida and Lee County produced three EF-0 landspout tornadoes during the afternoon that affected parts of Fort Myers and Cape Coral in Lee County.
episodes.213613: Clusters of showers and thunderstorms moved across portions of northwest Florida ahead of a frontal boundary. One storm produced a measured 82 mph wind gust on top of a landfill in Madison county.
episodes.213633: A cluster of severe storms occurred across portions of central MS during the evening hours of May 17, 2026. Strong winds caused multiple trees and powerlines to be blown down. Some of these storms had hail up to quarter size.
episodes.214253: A surge of warm and moist air aloft brought numerous thunderstorms to southern WI. One storm produced damaging winds in Sheboygan County.

A landspout tornado was observed at 3:17 PM EDT just to the east of U.S. Hwy 41/S Cleveland Ave and north of Woodland Blvd, where a citizen submitted video of a rotating cloud base and funnel near Wawa and Culver's, and later confirmed that they witnessed a ground circulation with surface and lofted dust and small debris. No significant damage was reported, and no other reports, pictures or videos have been confirmed indicating that the track extended beyond that location. Maximum estimated peak wind of 65 mph.

A landspout tornado that was likely associated with the circulation from a previous landspout that dissipated minutes earlier is estimated to have formed around 3:25 PM EDT approximately 1.75 miles to the northwest of the previous landspout, where damage was first noted along Reynard Ave in the Tanglewood area where a large tree had numerous medium to large branches snapped. Continuing northwest, branches and limbs were snapped at multiple locations across Cumberland and Woodwind Courts, and a home near Tanglewood Pkwy had a large tree uprooted in its yard. Additional footage was submitted from the Tanglewood area depicting lawn furniture and yard decor scattered about, along with fence and roof damage, and a video taken by a resident along Westminster Dr at 3:28 PM EDT showed airborne debris along with indications of the ground circulation as the landspout neared the McGregor Gardens area and Argyle Dr and McGregor Blvd. The circulation continued northwest across the Georgetown area just south of Colonial Blvd and began crossing the Caloosahatchee River just to the west-southwest of McGregor Colonial Memorial Park, and to the south of the Midpoint Bridge around 3:30 PM EDT. Videos taken by the public showed surface spray associated with the circulation as it approached and crossed the Midpoint Bridge west of McGregor Colonial Memorial Park and continued northwest toward the central section of the river north of the bridge, where it is estimated to have dissipated around 3:31 PM EDT before reaching the western shore of the river. Maximum estimated winds of 75 mph.

A landspout tornado formed over Cape Coral just north of the Sovereign Canal near SW 28th St around 3:35 PM EDT in association with a separate segment of the cluster of thunderstorms, with evidence of the circulation visible in video taken by residents along SW 4th Ave and SW 5th Ave. Footage from SW 4th Ave showed a pickup truck in the driveway of a home being displaced a number of feet as the circulation passed by the location, and footage from the SW 5th Ave location showed the funnel of the landspout and the surface circulation behind a home over the Niagara Canal. Additional footage of the circulation was taken approximately one-quarter mile to the northwest near the Seabell Canal, where footage from a home on the southern edge of the canal along SW 26th Ter showed the circulation blowing lawn chairs around and lofting additional unidentified debris, while also knocking over and blowing around vinyl fencing in the backyard of a home on the opposite/northern side of the canal along SW 26th St. A few additional reports and photos from the vicinity also indicated fence and some roof damage as the circulation neared the intersection of Skyline Blvd and Veterans Pkwy before it is estimated to have dissipated around 3:38 PM EDT, as no other reports, pictures or videos have been confirmed to indicate that the track extended further. Maximum estimated winds of 75 mph.
